:::note[Written against main]
This page follows `main` at 9a71121, and it differs from the copy in HotLoop core 4.18.11, the latest release. Parts of it may be newer than what you have installed. The [release notes](/releases/) say what moved.

For a Pi or a small industrial PC that is **not** part of a k3s cluster. If
it is, use the product's chart instead. This directory and the charts are the
two supported ways to run HotLoop.

No Docker, and no bare `podman run` from a shell that dies with the session.
Quadlet turns the containers into real systemd services: start on boot with
no user logged in, restart on failure, log to journald.

| Directory | Product | Image |
|---|---|---|
| `iot/` | HotLoop IoT, with PostgreSQL 17 | `ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-iot` |
| `edge/` | HotLoop Edge, with TimescaleDB | `ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-edge` |
| `gateway/` | HotLoop Gateway, with TimescaleDB | `ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop` |
| this directory | HotLoop Edge Relay, no database | `ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-edge-relay` |

[docs/PRODUCTS.md](/products/) says which one you want.

Each of the first three also has a `sqlite/` directory: the same product with
the database as a file and no database container. See
[SQLite instead of PostgreSQL](#sqlite-instead-of-postgresql).

## IoT, Edge and the Gateway

Each directory has the same units and one script:

- **`hotloop.network`**: the network the app and its database share. The app
  reaches the database by name (`hotloop-db:5432`) and nothing else on the box
  can, because the database publishes no port. Only the app's 8080 is
  published.
- **`hotloop.container`**: the app. Its header has the install steps; read it
  before copying anything.
- **`hotloop-db.container`**: the database, the same image and version that
  product's chart runs. It reports started once it answers, so the app waits
  for a database it can use.
- **`hotloop-db-upgrade.container`** and **`hotloop-db-upgrade.sh`**: the
  database's move from PostgreSQL 16 to 17, once. It runs before the database
  unit every time and does nothing unless the volume still holds 16 data. See
  [PostgreSQL 16 to 17](#postgresql-16-to-17).
- **`hotloop-db.volume`** and **`hotloop-data.volume`**: the database, and
  everything the app writes under `/data` (backups, certificates, the forward
  queue, reports). Named Podman volumes, so `podman system prune` leaves them
  alone.

Three Podman secrets hold what doesn't belong in a file:
`hotloop-db-password`, `hotloop-secret-key` (encrypts device passwords in the
database; keep a copy off the box) and `hotloop-admin-password-hash` (the
bcrypt hash of the first admin's password, never the password).

**Podman 5.0 or newer.** Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm ships Podman 4.3, which has
no Quadlet at all: use Raspberry Pi OS Trixie (Podman 5.4) or newer. The
updates below were run on Podman 6.1.3; the Edge Relay's unit, which shares the
same keys, on 4.9.3. And put the database volume on a USB SSD, not the SD card.
History writes all day, and SD cards die of exactly that.

### Why every product uses the same names

The unit names, the volume names and the secret names are identical in
`iot/`, `edge/` and `gateway/`, on purpose. Moving a box up a product is
copying the bigger product's `hotloop.container` and `hotloop-db.container`
over yours:

```sh
sudo cp gateway/hotloop.container gateway/hotloop-db.container \
  gateway/hotloop-db-upgrade.container gateway/hotloop-db-upgrade.sh /etc/containers/systemd/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart hotloop.service hotloop-db.service
```

The volumes and the secrets stay, and so does every device, tag, alarm, user
and hour of history. Back up first anyway (`POST /api/backup`). That move has
been run, IoT to Edge to the Gateway on one set of volumes. Going back down a
product hasn't been yet, so don't, on a box you care about.

It also means one HotLoop per box. Two would fight over port 8080 anyway.

### Verified

The shipped IoT, Edge, and Gateway files, untouched, generate under the `quadlet`
generator from Podman 6.1.3 with the same structure: the app requires the
database and the network, publishes its own port, carries the auto-update
label, and the database carries none and publishes nothing.

The Gateway's units were then run for real: rootless, under systemd, with a
local registry standing in for ghcr.io and the products' own `podman
auto-update`. A first start with the database coming up healthy and the app
healthy after it; an update to a release that adds a migration to a table the
app already uses, taken with the existing device and its data intact and the
database container never restarted; and an update to a release that migrates
the database and then can't start, which Podman rolled back, the previous
release starting healthy on the database the failed one had already migrated.
Edge and IoT were generated and compared, not run. Under systemd on a real
Pi: not yet.

## PostgreSQL 16 to 17

HotLoop's database is PostgreSQL 17 from this release. A box that ran an
earlier release has PostgreSQL 16 data, which PostgreSQL 17 will not open, so
the move is a unit that runs before the database. Get the new files in place and
restart the database, and that is all:

```sh
sudo cp hotloop-db.container hotloop-db-upgrade.container hotloop-db-upgrade.sh \
  /etc/containers/systemd/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart hotloop-db.service
journalctl -u hotloop-db-upgrade.service      # what it did
```

`hotloop-db.container` requires the upgrade unit, so a box that copied only the
new database unit does not start on 16 data and the journal says why. The
upgrade unit runs `pg_upgrade` in copy mode into a new directory beside the old
one, starts the new server once to prove it opens, and only then swaps the
names; the old data stays on the volume as `pgdata.pg16`. It pulls the
PostgreSQL 16 image only when the volume needs it. A failure leaves the 16 data
as it was and the database not started. The whole description, the way back and
how to delete `pgdata.pg16` are in
[DEPLOYMENT.md](/install/helm/#postgresql-17). For a rootless install
the script path in the unit is `~/.config/containers/systemd`, from `%E`.

## SQLite instead of PostgreSQL

The database is a setting, not an image (docs/DEPLOYMENT.md, "SQLite"). Under
Quadlet that means a second set of files, not a second image. Each product's
`sqlite/` directory has two:

- **`sqlite/hotloop.container`**: the app alone. No `Requires=` on a database,
  no network, no database password, and `HOTLOOP_DB_TYPE=sqlite` with the file
  at `HOTLOOP_DB_PATH=/data/hotloop.db`. It follows `:stable` and rolls back a
  bad update exactly like the PostgreSQL unit: same healthcheck, same
  `--sdnotify=healthy`.
- **`sqlite/hotloop-data.volume`**: the `hotloop-data` volume, which is where
  the database file and its `-wal` and `-shm` live. The same volume name as the
  PostgreSQL files', so it is the same data volume if you ever switch.

| Directory | Install | Secrets |
|---|---|---|
| `iot/`, `edge/`, `gateway/` | `hotloop.network`, `hotloop.container`, `hotloop-db.container`, `hotloop-db.volume`, `hotloop-data.volume` | three |
| `iot/sqlite/`, `edge/sqlite/`, `gateway/sqlite/` | `hotloop.container`, `hotloop-data.volume` | two: `hotloop-secret-key` and `hotloop-admin-password-hash` |

Install one set or the other, never both: they use the same unit names. The
header of `sqlite/hotloop.container` has the exact steps. In short:

```sh
cd iot/sqlite        # or edge/sqlite, gateway/sqlite
sudo cp hotloop.container hotloop-data.volume /etc/containers/systemd/
# make hotloop-secret-key and hotloop-admin-password-hash as the header says
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start hotloop.service
curl -s localhost:8080/api/status
```

A few things to know before you pick it. SQLite is one writer on one local
disk: a Pi puts the volume on a USB SSD, and network storage is not an option
because SQLite corrupts on it. History is one table with an index, not
partitions or a hypertable, so a site with years of history at one second wants
the PostgreSQL files. And moving a box between SQLite and PostgreSQL is a
backup and a restore ([BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/)), not a swap of units:
the new database starts empty. Do not copy a `sqlite/hotloop.container` over a
running PostgreSQL install to "switch"; the PostgreSQL volume's data is not
read by it.

Plain PostgreSQL on Edge or the Gateway is the TimescaleDB unit with
`Environment=HOTLOOP_HISTORIAN_TIMESCALE=false` added to `hotloop.container`.
IoT's unit is plain PostgreSQL already, and IoT has no TimescaleDB unit at all.

### Verified (SQLite)

`iot/sqlite/hotloop.container` and its volume were run rootless on Podman 4.9.3
under systemd (`systemctl --user`) from the committed files, changed only in the
names, the port, the image (built from the same tree) and the runtime directory
a user manager needs. The unit came up healthy, `/healthz` and `/readyz`
answered 200, the admin logged in from the hash secret, `/api/status` answered,
`hotloop.db`, `hotloop.db-wal` and `hotloop.db-shm` appeared on the volume,
and a restart applied no migrations and logged the admin in again. Edge and
Gateway `sqlite/` units are the same file apart from the image and the
retention default, and were checked by the guard, not run. Under systemd as
root on a real Pi: not yet.

## Edge Relay

- **`edge-relay-hold.conf`**: opt-in: hold image updates until an operator
  approves them. A systemd drop-in, not part of a default install.
- **`edge-relay.container`**, the service itself. Full install steps are in
  its own header comment; read it before copying anything.
- **`edge-relay-data.volume`**, a named Podman volume for the forward
  queue, so buffered readings survive a container restart. Podman creates it
  automatically the first time the service starts.
- **`devices.example.json`**, a starting point for the device file. Copy it
  to `/etc/edge-relay/devices.json` and edit it for the actual devices at
  this site, see [docs/EDGE-RELAY.md](/edge-relay/reference/) for the
  full format.

### Quick start

```sh
sudo mkdir -p /etc/containers/systemd /etc/edge-relay
sudo cp edge-relay.container edge-relay-data.volume /etc/containers/systemd/
sudo cp devices.example.json /etc/edge-relay/devices.json   # then edit it
sudo "$EDITOR" /etc/containers/systemd/edge-relay.container  # broker, group, node

# Skip this if the broker takes anonymous connections.
printf '%s' 'your-broker-password' | sudo podman secret create edge-relay-broker-password -

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start edge-relay.service
sudo systemctl status edge-relay.service
curl localhost:8081/status
```

**Updates.** The unit follows `:stable` and updates itself once Podman's timer
is on:

```sh
sudo systemctl enable --now podman-auto-update.timer
```

If a new image can't pass its healthcheck, Podman puts the old one back. The
Gateway's fleet list shows each relay's version and image digest and logs every
change. To hold updates until an admin approves them on the Gateway, install
`edge-relay-hold.conf` as the comment at the top of that file says, and turn the
timer off. Everything this does, and what it can't, is in
[docs/EDGE-RELAY.md](/edge-relay/reference/#updating-a-relay).

To pick up a change to the local file: edit it, then
`sudo systemctl restart edge-relay.service`. The relay reads that file at boot
and doesn't watch it.

A device file the Gateway pushes doesn't need any of that: it applies live,
without a restart. It can't be written to `/etc/edge-relay/devices.json`
(that's mounted `:ro` on a read-only root), so it goes on the data volume as
`/data/pushed-devices.json`, and while that exists it's what the relay runs
and boots from. Your edits to the local file sit there unused until you clear
the push: `DELETE /api/fleet/{id}/config` on the Gateway while the relay is
running, and it switches back to the local file on the spot. The journal
tells you which file it's on, so check there before you start doubting your
JSON.

Verified against the actual `quadlet` binary (`podman-5.8.6`'s
`/usr/libexec/podman/quadlet -dryrun`): both units parse cleanly and generate
the expected `podman run` invocation, with the volume dependency and secret
wired in automatically.
